issues.legal_issue: An insolvent may maintain a suit after absolute discharge to recover property that devolved on the insolvent while undischarged and remained undisposed of, subject to the property remaining liable for unpaid provable debts and insolvency expenses.
material_facts: The plaintiff was adjudged insolvent before the succession opened and received an absolute discharge afterward.
The property in dispute devolved on the plaintiff while the plaintiff was still undischarged.
The plaintiff sued after the absolute discharge to recover the property from persons in possession.
The property had not been disposed of in the insolvency proceedings.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiff could maintain the suit after absolute discharge. Undisposed property was surplus to which the discharged insolvent was entitled, subject to payment of any provable debts not already discharged and the expenses of the insolvency proceedings.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 28(2) and 28(4) of the Provincial Insolvency Act, property belonging to an insolvent, including property devolving during the period of undischarged insolvency, vests in the court or receiver. Reading the Act as a whole, section 67 entitles the insolvent to any surplus after creditors and proceeding expenses are paid; by necessary implication, undisposed property remaining at discharge is such surplus and the receiver's vesting ends, subject to those liabilities. Section 44(2) releases the insolvent from provable debts on discharge but does not itself expressly provide for revesting; section 37 expressly addresses revesting on annulment and does not govern discharge. Sections 41, 42 and 64 inform the scheme for discharge and final dividends. The Court discussed Sayad Daud Sayad Mohd. v. Mulna Mohd. Sayad, Yellavajjhula Surayya v. Tummalapalli Mangayya, Rup Narain Singh v. Har Gopal Tewari, Dewan Chand v. Manak Chand, Arjun Das Kundu v. Marchhiya Telinee, Kanshi Ram v. Hari Ram, and Parsu v. Balaji; it distinguished the English rule in Cohen v. Mitchel because the Indian Act expressly vests after-acquired or devolving property under section 28(4).

rule.if: post_discharge_property_recovery_suit and absolute_discharge_granted and property_devolved_while_undischarged and property_undisposed_at_discharge

predicates.post_discharge_property_recovery_suit: The proceeding is a suit brought after discharge to recover property from a person in possession.
predicates.absolute_discharge_granted: The court granted the insolvent an absolute discharge.
predicates.property_devolved_while_undischarged: The property devolved on the insolvent while the insolvent remained undischarged.
predicates.property_undisposed_at_discharge: The property remained undisposed of in the insolvency proceedings when discharge was granted.

issues.definition: When an insolvent brings a property-recovery suit after absolute discharge for property that devolved during undischarged insolvency and remained undisposed of, the insolvent may recover it subject to unpaid insolvency liabilities.

issues.legal_issue: A testamentary grant that limits a beneficiary to enjoyment during life of income from property confers a life estate when the will as a whole confirms that limited intention.
material_facts: The will gave property to each widow and stated that she could enjoy the income as owner during her lifetime.
For one widow's property, the will expressly limited her enjoyment to the income.
The will directed that an adopted son would become entitled to the properties after the widows' deaths.
Elsewhere, the will used different and more explicit language when making an absolute bequest.
issues.conclusion: The bequests of the relevant properties to the widows conferred life estates, not absolute estates.
issues.legal_principle: A will must be construed as a whole, considering surrounding circumstances and contrasting its clauses to ascertain the testator's intention. The words describing enjoyment as owner do not confer an absolute estate when the clause limits enjoyment to income during the beneficiary's lifetime; the remainder provision and contrasting language used for an absolute bequest reinforce that limitation. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this construction.

rule.if: will_construction_proceeding and lifetime_income_limited and (remainder_after_beneficiary_life or absolute_bequest_contrasted)

predicates.will_construction_proceeding: The dispute requires a court to determine the nature of an interest created by a will.
predicates.lifetime_income_limited: The will limits the beneficiary's enjoyment to income from the property during the beneficiary's lifetime.
predicates.remainder_after_beneficiary_life: The will provides that another person becomes entitled to the property after the beneficiary's death.
predicates.absolute_bequest_contrasted: The will uses materially different, explicit language to give an absolute estate elsewhere.

issues.definition: In a will-construction proceeding, a lifetime limit on income, supported by a remainder provision or contrasting absolute-bequest language, results in a life estate for the beneficiary.

issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate as a whole when the heirs of a deceased defendant connected with one property are not substituted in time if the interests in the other properties are independent, though the appeal abates as to the deceased defendant's inseparable property interest.
material_facts: One defendant died after the High Court decree, and the application to substitute that defendant's heirs was not made within the prescribed time.
The deceased defendant and another purchaser held one property jointly, and the record did not establish that their interests were separate and distinct.
The interests of the defendants possessing the other properties were independent.
issues.conclusion: The appeal abated as to the jointly held property connected with the deceased defendant, but it did not abate as a whole and could proceed concerning the other properties.
issues.legal_principle: Where defendants' interests in different properties are independent, the failure to bring the heirs of a deceased defendant on the record within time does not cause the entire appeal to abate. If the deceased defendant's interest in a particular property is joint and not shown to be separate and severable from a co-owner's interest, abatement applies to that property. The Court relied on no statutory provision or earlier case for this procedural ruling.

rule.if: appeal_with_deceased_party and substitution_not_timely and independent_interests_in_other_properties and joint_property_interest_not_shown_severable

predicates.appeal_with_deceased_party: The proceeding is an appeal in which a party has died.
predicates.substitution_not_timely: The deceased party's heirs were not substituted within the time allowed.
predicates.independent_interests_in_other_propertie: The other defendants' interests in other properties are independent of the deceased party's interest.
predicates.joint_property_interest_not_shown_severa: The deceased party held a property jointly with another person, and the joint interests were not shown to be separate and distinct.

issues.definition: When substitution is late in an appeal, independent property interests allow the appeal to continue as to those properties, while an inseparable property interest connected to the deceased party abates.
